items.title: Motion to Reconvene into Open Session
Charlene Lee, Mauleek Bhatt, and Eddie Grignon, Lived Expertise Engagement Program - Social Development Centre
notes:
Charlene Lee, Mauleek Bhatt, and Eddie Grignon provided a presentation that reviewed 30 calls to action that were provided to Council by the Lived Expertise Engagement Program after the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness (PECH) was approved. A copy of the presentation is attached to the agenda. They highlighted progress on calls to action across the categories of Centre Community Voices, Focus on Preventing Homelessness, Create Policy and System Accountability, Build System Bridges, Advance Equitable Housing, Change the Narrative on Housing, Advocate and Collaborate for Broader Change, and Climate and Extreme Weather Planning.

In response to the Committee, C. Lee confirmed that the Lived Expertise Engagement Program is the only remaining local lived expertise advisory group and noted previous groups and programs that have ended due to lack of funding.

In response to the Committee, E. Grignon described what a memorialization process could look like to remember individuals experiencing homelessness who have passed away and acknowledged the necessity of outlets for grief in the community.

The Committee encouraged the delegates to share their perspectives with Committee members regularly.

The Committee also noted that there is a need for a culturally responsive element when addressing housing and homelessness.

In response to the Committee, C. Lee explained that an ideal homelessness advocacy office would offer centralized social support services and dedicated support workers to follow each individual client's journey in order to build relationships and minimize trauma.

items.title: CSD-HOU-26-008, 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan, 2026-2036
notes:
Ryan Pettipiere, Director, Housing Services provided a joint introduction to reports under 7.1.1 and 7.1.2. He noted that together, these reports provide both a long-term roadmap and a progress update on housing and homelessness in the Region. He highlighted that community members are at the centre of the reports and that data guides action items and planning for the future. He also highlighted that there has been a recent flattening of the homelessness curve, and for the first time, housing outcomes are outpacing the inflow into chronic homelessness. He further noted that there will be serious future challenges without strengthened and sustained investment in housing and homelessness solutions. 

R. Pettipiere shared the story of a community member who was able to transition from homelessness into supportive housing after connecting with support workers and wraparound services. He placed emphasis on the effectiveness and necessity of comprehensive supportive services, highlighting that the available data demonstrates that the challenges that individuals experiencing homelessness face can be mitigated with effective services.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere noted that the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan is a provincially legislated responsibility of Service System Managers and that the Region follows a provincial mandate on the scope of the Plan and the timeline for the approval process.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that the PATHS2HOME program no longer exists but acknowledged that several of the beneficial elements from PATHS2HOME now exist within other current Regional programs. He also noted that staff can continue to look for available resources to reimplement the PATHS2HOME program if evidence suggests that reimplementation would be beneficial for the community.

R. Pettipiere clarified that the Provincial government has approved the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan but that approval from Council is necessary in order to proceed with implementation. He noted that the previous 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan has now expired and if Council defers approval of the new Plan until the next term of Council, this will create a limbo state in terms of staff being able to move forward with work within the new Plan.

Peter Sweeney, Commissioner, Community Services, confirmed that the Plan is a directional plan and does not commit resources. Staff will align any resources that are allocated through the budget process with the direction of the Plan.

R. Pettipiere clarified that targets for measurable KPIs will be determined once annual service levels are determined by funding allocations during the budget process.

In response to the Committee, P. Sweeney confirmed that the Region is actively engaged in conversations with the Provincial government surrounding housing and homelessness and noted the importance of a holistic approach to addressing these issues that includes the healthcare sector and other community partners.

P. Sweeney also confirmed that future reports to Council can include additional data and metrics to measurably demonstrate staff's work in addressing housing and homelessness.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere noted that the Housing Needs Assessment can help to determine what housing typologies are needed within the area municipalities to assist with meaningful planning for the future.

R. Pettipiere also noted that the Plan outlines areas where more focus and resources are needed to address housing and homelessness, including rural townships, Indigenous people, lone parent households, and seniors.

P. Sweeney indicated that a 2027 reimagining of Building Better Futures will incorporate the Region's Seniors' Services division to assist with determining further actions to support seniors.

R. Pettipiere noted that while the specific reports at hand do not include a demographic breakdown of the population experiencing chronic homelessness, the Point in Time count does collect additional data, including underlying causes of homelessness, that is tracked. He also noted that the Region tracks the acuity of chronic homelessness and tri-morbidities, emphasizing that wraparound supports and the right kinds of supportive housing are critical in achieving successful retention housing rates, with the Region currently achieving a retention rate of approximately 98-99%.

R. Pettipiere indicated that the Region has completed a Housing Needs Assessment and next steps include calculating costs associated with providing housing to meet projected needs.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that bottlenecks exist throughout all stages on the housing continuum, and that increased market housing rates increase backlogs on the rest of continuum and puts increasing pressure on the affordable housing waitlist.

R. Pettipiere also clarified that while a significant portion of actions within the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness are currently underway, there are also a significant portion of these actions that will be continuously ongoing or will never end up completed due to lack of resources.

In response to the Committee, R. Pettipiere noted that the 10 Year Housing and Homelessness Plan outlines steps to move away from emergency responses to housing and homelessness and towards solving these issues and implementing preventative measures, further noting that strengthened and ongoing investments will be needed to move in this direction.

In response to the Committee, P. Sweeney noted that orientation for the next term of Council can take into consideration building greater awareness and connection with the community groups collaboratively involved in housing and homelessness work.

R. Pettipiere noted that a housing and homelessness strategy for youth has been restricted by a lack of staff capacity to take this work on, but as other work is finishing, staff can shift resources once new priorities are established for next year as part of upcoming meetings with the Co-Creators Group. He also noted that the Region could have an effective role in a youth strategy by acting as a coordinator for the work of various youth organizations that already exist within the Region.

In response to the Committee, P. Sweeney confirmed that staff will note Council's interest in being presented with disaggregated demographic data as part of future reporting on the expected future demands for housing supports and noted again the importance of integrating housing work with the healthcare system. 

In response to the questions from the Committee regarding OW and ODSP rates, P. Sweeney underscored that the causes of chronic homelessness are multi-factoral, noting that during the last Point in Time count in 2024, individuals identified income as the top factor that had resulted in their homelessness. He also noted that chronic homelessness cannot be addressed without also addressing economic insecurity and poverty.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
PHP-IDS-26-002, Integrated Public Health School Services and Partnerships
notes:
Dr. Hsiu-Li Wang, Commissioner, Public Health and Paramedic Services and Medical Officer of Health, introduced the report and provided an update on Public Health's school-based services, including the enforcement of the Immunization of School Pupils Act (ISPA), grade seven immunization clinics, universal dental screening and case management, visual health promotion, sexual health education and referrals, substance use prevention, and student well-being supports. She noted that important outcomes from the 2025-2026 school year included the increase of student immunization record compliance from approximately 85% to more than 98%, 19,100 vaccine doses administered in schools, and over 19,000 students being screened in the oral health screening program, with 5.4% of students having urgent dental care needs. She emphasized the importance of school-based screening programs to identify needs that might otherwise go unaddressed.

Dr. Wang also noted that coordination between Public Health programs and schools to operate these programs allows for streamlining of communications, supports efficient use of staff resources, makes navigating public health services easier for schools and families, supports early intervention and preparedness for emerging health risks, and promotes the health and well-being of youth.

Received for information.
